title: Polygon visibility graph recognition
formal: Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a finite simple undirected graph \(G\) on \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and a cyclic order \(C=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) of its vertices, decides whether some simple polygon with these labelled vertices in boundary order \(C\) has visibility graph exactly \(G\)? Here \(n\geq3\), the graph is given by its complete adjacency matrix and the cyclic order by an explicit list. Both visible and nonvisible pairs must be realized, and the polygon has no holes or additional vertices.
why: The problem is a central inverse question about geometric visibility: whether pairwise sight-line information and a boundary order can be tested for realizability efficiently. It connects graph recognition with geometric representation complexity.
status_note: The specified fixed-order recognition question remains explicitly open in the checked 2024 compendium. The bounded search through 13 September 2026 did not locate a later resolution. Closed visibility and permitted collinear labelled vertices are explicit formulation conventions; no unrestricted rational-witness assumption is used.

progress.text: Lin and Skiena investigate representation complexity and its bearing on short recognition certificates.
The Open Problems Project lists the fixed-boundary-order polynomial recognition question.
The compendium explicitly states that recognition remains open even with boundary order given.

importance.reason: A longstanding graph-realization problem whose difficulty persists even with the polygon boundary order fixed; it tests the boundary between combinatorial recognition and real-coordinate geometry.

sentences: A polygon's visibility graph records which pairs of vertices can be joined by a segment lying inside the polygon.
The source supplies both a candidate graph and a Hamiltonian cycle specifying the intended polygon boundary.
It asks for an efficient decision procedure for whether a simple polygon realizes exactly that information.
Choosing coordinates must satisfy visibility and obstruction requirements simultaneously.
The problem tests whether a combinatorial record of sight lines contains enough accessible structure to reconstruct a genuine geometric environment.

definitions: A realization assigns distinct points \(p_i\in\mathbb R^2\) to the labels. The union of the segments \([p_{v_i},p_{v_{i+1}}]\), with indices cyclic modulo \(n\), must be a simple closed polygonal curve: consecutive segments meet only at their common endpoint and nonconsecutive segments are disjoint. Let \(P\) be this curve together with its bounded complementary component. Vertices \(i\ne j\) are visible exactly when the entire closed segment \([p_i,p_j]\) is contained in \(P\). Visibility along the boundary is allowed, including through other labelled collinear vertices; redundant collinear boundary vertices are permitted as long as the curve remains simple. This closed-region convention is explicit and no general-position promise is imposed. The graph must contain every edge of the specified boundary cycle, otherwise the answer is no. Malformed matrices, a nonsymmetric matrix, loops, a nonpermutation order or \(n<3\) are rejected. The input is a binary encoding of the full matrix and list, of length \(N\); one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine must decide correctly in at most \(K(N+1)^a\) steps for fixed \(K,a\). Real coordinates are existential mathematical witnesses, with no rationality, grid-size or bit-length restriction. The requested algorithm returns a Boolean answer and need not produce coordinates.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the language of realizable graph/order pairs belongs to \(\mathrm P\), or that it does not, for the exact polygon and visibility conventions above. A positive answer must establish correctness and a polynomial worst-case bit-time bound for one uniform decision algorithm on every encoding. A negative answer must rule out every such algorithm; an NP-hardness or \(\exists\mathbb R\)-hardness result alone does not prove nonmembership in \(\mathrm P\) without the corresponding separation. A necessary graph condition, recognition of a special polygon class, or recognition with extra geometric data is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: The source problem supplies the boundary order as well as the graph. This removes the need to search for a Hamiltonian boundary cycle, but leaves the geometric realizability question. The statement above fixes simple closed polygons and closed-segment visibility explicitly.

Constructing the visibility graph of an already drawn polygon and recognizing a graph that could arise from some polygon are different tasks. Recognition has to account simultaneously for every edge and every absent edge without being given any coordinates.

The 2024 compendium by Schaefer, Cardinal and Miltzow explicitly retains polygon visibility recognition as open even when the boundary order is supplied. It defines visibility by containment of the complete joining segment in the polygon.

The same compendium distinguishes several related recognition problems with \(\exists\mathbb R\) hardness or completeness results, including polygons with holes and simultaneous interior/exterior visibility. Those results impose different objects or additional data and do not settle this simple-polygon problem. Here \(\exists\mathbb R\) denotes problems reducible in polynomial time to the existence of real solutions of finite systems of polynomial equalities and inequalities.

Lin and Skiena study coordinate requirements for realizing visibility graphs. The fact that a realization is a finite list of real points does not by itself make it a polynomial-length certificate in the Turing model.

A polynomial algorithm would identify when a purely combinatorial collection of sight lines can come from one polygonal environment. The fixed boundary order is part of the scientific question; discarding it or requiring a convex polygon would change the class being recognized.
